extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and math researchers writing abstracts/intros for a general audience (including early-career authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Produce a concise, non-technical abstract and story-like introduction for mathematical work that is clear, engaging, and curiosity-inducing—short enough to work as a tweet yet compelling enough to motivate deeper reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-technical abstract (tweet-length yet compelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a non-technical abstract of your math work that is concise enough for a tweet yet compelling enough to spark curiosity about the full details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core recommendation from the page: the abstract should be short (tweet-length) and non-technical, but still interesting enough to make readers want to learn more. This is the primary deliverable to aim for when 'telling a mathematical story.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Short and to the point
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the story tightly focused on the key idea(s). Avoid extraneous technical detail; present only what is necessary to convey the core message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straightforward (clear for general audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear enough for a general audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain language and simple structure so non-specialists can follow the main point. Avoid jargon or, if unavoidable, explain it briefly in intuitive terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting (shareable/engaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging enough that someone would want to share it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the work to highlight conflict, novelty, or surprising insight that makes the audience care. Think of social-shareability as a proxy for accessibility and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity-inducing (leaves audience wanting more)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude the short story/abstract with enough mystery or open question to motivate readers to seek the full paper or details, without promising misleading simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept the inherent tension of distillation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Distilled products always lack flavor compared to the real thing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that simplification will omit nuance; that's acceptable provided the distilled story nonetheless contains enough intrigue to motivate deeper exploration. Avoid over-simplifying to the point of misrepresenting the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use compact narrative models (examples)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate tight narrative devices: Aesop's fable reduces a story to an essential moral; the Terminator tagline captures core conflict in a sentence. Use such models to craft a one-sentence hook or moral for your math story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clarity while distilling complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling complex ideas into their most essential and engaging form without sacrificing clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The storytelling task is distinct from fiction: be ruthless in removing extraneous detail but ensure the remaining phrasing truthfully conveys the idea. Clarity must not be sacrificed for brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the paper's abstract and introduction function as story elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' math paper is one whose abstract works as a tweet and whose introduction works as a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the abstract as the short hook and the introduction as the expanded narrative that tells the motivation/conflict and entices the reader into proofs. These are communicative skills separate from proving results.
